## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

_Why does a better model not, by itself, make a better machine?_

The learned model is the part of a physical machine that is easiest to improve and easiest to score, so it attracts most of the effort. Useful service depends on everything around it as well. The body must sustain the task across loads, surfaces, and hours of duty, the learned behavior must hold in the states its own actions create, each proposal must be admitted, corrected, or refused before the motion it asks for is already under way, and the evidence for all of it must match the conditions of operation and stay true as the machine and its site change. Each of these can be engineered well in isolation while the machine as a whole remains unjustified, because doubt accumulates across every premise a physical claim depends on, and a premise that no one names or owns is assumed silently. A team that cannot join these parts into one argument keeps improving the model while an unmeasured floor, an unqualified detector, or an unowned restriction decides what the machine actually does. The same joined argument also chooses what to build next, since the most valuable measurement, experience, or design change is the one that retires the weakest open premise. At the causal boundary, irreversibility makes that weakest premise, not the best prediction, the measure of what a machine may be trusted to do.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Explain why a better prediction can still produce a worse physical action, and synthesize the four laws into the design argument that answers it
- Place current learned proposers in the move from prediction to action, and explain why more capable proposers do not move the permission decision into the model
- Apply the four laws to select and evaluate a candidate operating mode for an unfamiliar machine
- Distinguish proposer autonomy, whole-machine task success, and protection when assessing a completed design
- Construct residual-claims entries with supported restrictions, accountable owners, and predeclared closure tests
- Select the next measurement, learning experiment, or design change needed to extend a machine's capability
:::

## From a Better Prediction to Useful Service {#sec-frontier-architectural-synthesis}

Each part of this book established one kind of claim about a machine whose learned outputs become physical actions: what its body can sustain, what its learned proposer has shown, what its runtime admits in time, and what its evidence licenses. The chapters built those claims one at a time, and a concluding synthesis must show three things that no single chapter could. The claims must join into one argument on the machine they were built around. The method must transfer to a machine the book never discussed. Because physical work cannot be undone, the argument must also state what it does not yet support, since an unstated premise is the one most likely to be spent in the field. @Sec-boundary asked why a better prediction can still produce a worse physical action, and what the rest of the machine must supply so that a learned proposal becomes useful work within justified limits. That is the book's central question. This section answers it for the warehouse machine and places the answer in the longer move from prediction to action. @Sec-frontier-generalizing-unfamiliar-systems then carries the method to a packaging cell, @sec-frontier-epistemic-limits records the premises that no sensor on either machine reports, and @sec-frontier-assumptions-change turns those open premises into the choice of the next capability.

The argument ran on one machine, whose mission was to collect an object from a conveyor, open a spring-latched cage door, and carry a load through an aisle shared with people. Completing that mission requires the abilities promised in @sec-boundary, to design, teach, integrate, evaluate, and maintain a machine within justified limits, and the four parts developed them on this machine, with each choice constraining the next.

The first half of the question now has a precise answer. A better prediction can produce a worse action because the action is judged by quantities the prediction does not contain. The distance the body travels while the model computes, the friction the floor supplies under braking, the states the proposer's own actions lead it into, and the conditions under which its evidence was gathered all decide what a command does once it crosses the causal boundary, and none of them is an input to the model. Improving the model improves the proposal without changing any of those quantities.

The second half, what the rest of the machine must supply, is the four-step argument of @sec-boundary-central-question, one step per law, and each part supplied its step on this machine. Under the first law, irreversibility, the body's physical limits bound what any proposal may ask for. Part I turned load, traction, contact force, heat, and energy into the budgets that bound proposal size, cadence, and the independent execution path. Under the second law, endogenous data, the proposer's competence holds only over the states its data and evaluation covered, and its own actions choose those states. Part II tied the candidate proposer to the states it actually visits, so that a failed recovery becomes the next collection target rather than an anomaly. Under the third law, proposal is not permission, an independent permission path rather than the model decides what executes. Part III joined observation age, grounded goals, timed trajectories, and admission into one pick that placement keeps feasible under load. Under the fourth law, evidence bounds authority, the evidence gathered about the whole machine bounds where it may operate. Part IV turned execution into a service decision in which proposer autonomy, whole-machine success, and protection remain separate outcomes. A least-change speed correction can preserve a successful delivery even though the raw proposal needed intervention, while an emergency rescue does not by itself demonstrate service. @Tbl-17-master-synthesis collects the records that carry each of these results forward.

On the running machine, the answer takes the form of a release decision rather than a claim of success. The actual illustrative records in @sec-release-case-worked-full still yield `REFUSE`. The separately stipulated branch in @sec-release-stipulated-service shows how supporting evidence would change that decision to `COND`. Under its assumed task-performance and fault evidence, the machine may carry out restricted inspected-route mug delivery, the guarded door approach, and local handover, while its standing floor, crossing, feed, and calibration conditions hold. This is a worked engineering result under stated premises, not a report of a qualified deployment. Its value is the complete connection from a useful mission to the evidence and operating conditions that would support it.

@Fig-17-causal-loop-synthesis returns to the five-level machine introduced at the beginning of the book. The Brain proposes, the permission path admits, modifies, or refuses, and the Body delivers the admitted command across the Boundary into a World that continues evolving. Measurements return with their capture times. Release governs the configuration and standing conditions; it does not replace the live permission decision.

```{python}
#| label: calc-frontier-loop-figure
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CLOSED-LOOP SYNTHESIS FIGURE LABELS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-17-causal-loop-synthesis (SVG labels are hand-typed).
# │ Goal:    Keep the machine's rates and bus voltage drawn in the figure
# │          equal to the registry values the rest of the book prints.
# │ Show:    Nothing; the cell only guards the drawn labels.
# │ How:     Compare each drawn label with the registered machine value.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class LoopSynthesisFigure:
    """Values drawn in fig17_closed_loop_synthesis.svg."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Drawn labels and the registry values they must match) ──────
    drawn = {
        "intent rate (Hz)": (2.0, RM.intent_rate.to(ureg.Hz).magnitude),
        "intent inference (ms)": (336.0, RM.intent_reference_latency.to(ureg.ms).magnitude),
        "chunk renewal (ms)": (50.0, (1 / RM.chunk_rate).to(ureg.ms).magnitude),
        "setpoint step (ms)": (25.0, RM.chunk_step.to(ureg.ms).magnitude),
        "permission tick (kHz)": (1.0, RM.permission_rate.to(ureg.kHz).magnitude),
        "drive bus nominal (V)": (47.7, RM.drive_bus_nominal.to(ureg.volt).magnitude),
        "drive current loop (kHz)": (20.0, RM.current_loop_rate.to(ureg.kHz).magnitude),
    }

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    for _name, (_label, _value) in drawn.items():
        check(abs(_label - _value) < 1e-9, f"closed-loop figure label for {_name} is stale ({_label} vs {_value})")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    intent_rate_str = fmt_frequency(RM.intent_rate, unit=ureg.Hz, precision=0)
    renewal_str = fmt_latency(1 / RM.chunk_rate, unit=ureg.ms, precision=0)
    setpoint_str = fmt_latency(RM.chunk_step, unit=ureg.ms, precision=0)
    permission_str = fmt_frequency(RM.permission_rate, unit=ureg.kHz, precision=0)
    bus_str = fmt_voltage(RM.drive_bus_nominal, precision=1)
    current_loop_str = fmt_frequency(RM.current_loop_rate, unit=ureg.kHz, precision=0)
```

The Body's current becomes force and motion at the Boundary, the World evolves, and the Boundary returns measurements with capture times to the permission path and the Brain. Labels give the intent model 2 Hz with 336 ms inference, chunk renewal every 50 ms, a setpoint every 25 ms, a 1 kHz permission tick, a 20 kHz current loop in the drives, and a 47.7 V drive bus; the Boundary is event-timed, the World is continuous, and governance has no control rate."}
