|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Braking traction**: every aisle floor supplies $\mu \ge$ `{python} OilFilm.mu_min_str`; friction beneath a clear film is unobserved. | At $\mu$ = `{python} OilFilm.mu_oil_str` the credible deceleration falls to `{python} OilFilm.a_oil_str`, and the incomplete known-component budget at `{python} OilFilm.v_aisle_str` already grows to `{python} OilFilm.stop_oil_str` against a `{python} OilFilm.d_clear_str` clear distance. | Candidate in the actual records: `{python} OilFilm.v_restricted_str` on qualified, controlled floors ($\mu \ge$ `{python} OilFilm.mu_insp_str`); full timing and reserve must support it. Uncontrolled routes excluded. *Owner*: site operations, through the spill procedure for pallet-jack routes.                   | A floor-film detector with a miss rate of at most `{python} OilFilm.p_miss_target_sym_str` at `{python} OilFilm.confidence_sym_str` confidence, from `{python} OilFilm.n_closure_str` failure-free seeded-film trials, plus timing and clearance tests; the restriction holds until it passes.                               |
| **Walking person**: no person approaches the rack end during a stop; presence in the hidden cross aisle is unobserved.                 | A person walking at `{python} OilFilm.v_h_str` through the whole stop would cap the base far below its aisle speed at the rack end (@sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes).                                                                                                                       | Controlled separation excluding continuing human approach during a stop; no credit for an unqualified presence sensor. *Owner*: site operations.                                                                                                                                                                        | Qualify coverage, detection timing, and the complete response; `{python} OilFilm.n_closure_str` failure-free trials support a `{python} OilFilm.p_miss_target_sym_str` miss bound at `{python} OilFilm.confidence_sym_str` confidence for the declared trial population.                                                     |
| **Object identity**: the object grasped is the object the task names; identity and fragility before contact are unobserved.            | A confident grounding to a thin-walled glass jar beside the red mug passes every geometric check, and a grip the ceramic mug needs can crush the glass.                                                                                                                                         | Feed control admits to the conveyor only items on the station's declared list, none of them a fragile look-alike; singulation admits a grasp only with one object in the pick window. An off-list item arriving alone is contained only by the feed procedure. *Owner*: site operations, jointly with the task profile. | A qualified identity check at the station (tag read or scale-and-code) with a false-accept rate of at most `{python} OilFilm.p_miss_target_sym_str` at `{python} OilFilm.confidence_sym_str` confidence, from `{python} OilFilm.n_closure_str` failure-free seeded look-alike trials; the restriction holds until it passes. |

: **Residual-claims register for the aisle and the pick station**: Proposed responses to three open premises behind the mobile manipulator's aisle speed and its pick; operating credit requires the supporting evidence stipulated in the restricted-service branch. For each, the register names the missing physical observable, the hazard it permits, the operating restriction and its accountable owner, and the predeclared closure test that would retire the restriction. {#tbl-17-claims-register tbl-colwidths="[22,24,26,28]"}

The register also retains the timing premise from @sec-placement. Capture-to-dispatch age does not include dispatch-to-admission work, so @sec-placement allocates that interval separately, `{python} OilFilm.delta_da_str` of the `{python} OilFilm.t_latest_str` timing allowance at the aisle speed, which leaves `{python} OilFilm.reserve_da_str` of reserve. The allocation is a budget, not a measurement, and nominal inference cadence does not bound the interval between successful admissions. The runtime team owns a loaded qualification of both intervals against the handoff record's lease and renewal requirements. Until that evidence confirms the allocation and its positive reserve, the normal aisle speed remains a candidate. The stipulated service branch assumes supporting timing evidence for its restricted mode; it does not close this item in the actual records.

A release pipeline records each entry in a fixed schema, and its fields, units, and invariants appear with the other record layouts in @sec-appendix-systems-wire-residual-claims.

#### Maintaining the restrictions {#sec-frontier-operationalizing-claims}

The restrictions in the register must reach the mechanisms that govern deployment and execution. A signed speed ceiling constrains the permission path; an inspection requirement constrains site operations. The release pipeline checks that both belong to the authorized configuration, while runtime monitors check only those conditions their sensors can establish. An unobserved premise cannot become a measured condition merely because it appears in a machine-readable record.

An updated model or configuration must retain every standing restriction whose supporting claim remains unchanged. The deployment gate validates the signed limits and the evidence status before authorizing a mode. A restricted mode needs its own supported release; an open entry does not automatically authorize a downgrade. Runtime checks can enforce the speed ceiling and current authority, while site operations maintains the floor and feed procedures at their specified cadences.

The selected fallback remains the state-dependent response qualified in @sec-enforcement. A rejected replacement proposal need not revoke an active command whose own evidence, lease, and state remain valid. Loss of active permission does require a feasible response within the remaining budget. Powered deceleration, brake application at standstill, torque inhibit, and supply isolation have different physical effects; the register cannot replace those distinctions with a universal cutoff recipe.

The proposed detectors would support broader online claims only after qualification. Conservative actions, passive limits, proof tests, or a narrower task may support different claims without resolving every hidden state. Choosing among these responses requires checking what can still happen before the physical deadline.

### Failures without detectors {#sec-frontier-failures-without-detectors}

A floor-film detector can change the friction claim only if its coverage, false alarms, and response timing support the intended route. These are task-specific acceptance criteria, not universal detector thresholds. The known-component stopping calculation leaves `{python} OilFilm.spare_aisle_str` at the candidate normal aisle speed, equivalent to `{python} OilFilm.t_latest_str` of added delay; the `{python} OilFilm.delta_da_str` dispatch-to-admission allocation leaves `{python} OilFilm.reserve_da_str` of it before the required reserve is preserved. This is an upper limit on unallocated time, not a qualified detector budget. It also cannot establish protection against a person who continues approaching throughout the stop.

The floor-film detector faces an even stricter form of the same test. Its forward detection distance, less the travel incurred during its own sensing and inference latency, must cover the dry-floor stop to the film's leading edge:
$$d_{\text{detect}} \ge v\,t_{\text{detect}} + d_{\text{budget}}(v),$$
where $d_{\text{budget}}(v)$ is the finished dry-floor budget of @tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget. With a chosen detector latency of `{python} OilFilm.t_detect_str` at `{python} OilFilm.v_aisle_str`, the detector must report the film at least `{python} OilFilm.d_detect_min_str` ahead. That is essentially the rack end's whole `{python} OilFilm.d_clear_str` clear distance, because the chosen latency consumes almost all of the `{python} OilFilm.t_latest_str` computed above, and it leaves far too little for the `{python} OilFilm.delta_da_str` dispatch-to-admission allocation. A classification report that arrives once the drive wheels have already crossed onto the film leaves an incomplete stopping budget already at `{python} OilFilm.stop_oil_str` against the `{python} OilFilm.d_clear_str` clear distance. A classification received after that point supports incident diagnosis, but it cannot safeguard the action already taken.

#### Observational indistinguishability and the action deadline {#sec-frontier-observational-indistinguishability-sub}

The fundamental physical limit of runtime detection arises from observational indistinguishability. Consider two physical states of the world, $S_A$ and $S_B$. In state $S_A$, a commanded actuator trajectory $u(t)$ is completely safe. In state $S_B$, the identical trajectory $u(t)$ causes catastrophic structural fracture or human injury, requiring the permission path to intervene and command an immediate stop. What bounds the response is distance, not time. Braking changes the trajectory, so the harm point is a place. Let $d_{\text{rem}}$ be the distance remaining to it when the distinguishing observation arrives. The stop completes short of it only if
$$d_{\text{rem}} \ge v\,(t_{\text{enforce}} + t_{\text{actuation}}) + d_{\text{brake}}(v),$$
the same stopping model the book has used since @sec-body, with $d_{\text{brake}}(v)$ the selected stop's braking distance. Dividing by the approach speed turns it into a deadline on the observation time, $t_{\text{deadline}} = t_{\text{harm}} - t_{\text{enforce}} - t_{\text{actuation}} - d_{\text{brake}}(v)/v$, where $t_{\text{harm}}$ is the time the unchanged trajectory would reach the harm point. A tempting time-domain version subtracts the full braking duration $t_{\text{brake}}$ instead of $d_{\text{brake}}/v$, as if the machine kept its speed until it stopped. For the aisle's jerk-limited stop from `{python} OilFilm.v_aisle_str`, the stop lasts `{python} OilFilm.t_brake_aisle_str` but covers only the distance of `{python} OilFilm.t_brake_equiv_str` at constant speed, so the time form over-reserves `{python} OilFilm.t_overreserve_str`, or `{python} OilFilm.d_overreserve_str` of travel, more than the whole `{python} OilFilm.spare_aisle_str` spare. Contact adds its own coupled model: once the tool touches a stiff latch, force rather than position sets the deadline (@sec-enforcement-intentional-contact).

If the telemetry history $y(t)$ is identical for $S_A$ and $S_B$ until $t_{\text{deadline}}$ for every admissible input the machine could apply, no algorithm operating on those observations can distinguish the benign state from the hazardous one, and a state-specific response before that deadline is ruled out. The qualifier matters. Distinguishability depends on the input, as nonlinear observability makes precise [@hermann1977nonlinear], and an engineer can sometimes choose an input that separates the states. That choice is **active probing**\index{Active probing}, the idea behind auxiliary signal design for failure detection [@campbell2004auxiliary]: a controlled pull on the latch below the contact ceiling, or a small torque pulse on a known patch of floor, turns a hidden premise into an observation. Its cost is time and a small, bounded excitation that must itself fit the envelope. Where no admissible probe separates the states in time, a conservative action chosen for both states or a passive mechanical limit may still protect them, if its own clearance and force assumptions are valid.

#### Responses when the state remains hidden {#sec-frontier-passive-compliance-containment}

When physical states are observationally indistinguishable before the deadline, software cannot choose a different response for each state. Four responses remain. An admissible probe can make the states distinguishable in time, and a conservative action valid in both states can still be admitted. Where neither exists, mechanical compliance, physical proof-testing, or structural isolation must establish a supported operating envelope, or operation must be withheld.

Sensing hardware shows the same limit over longer durations. A robot's strain-gauge wrist force-torque transducer can drift as mechanical stress relaxation and temperature cycles affect its bridge output, and a transducer whose zero has drifted low reports the same trend as an interaction that genuinely exerts lower contact force. A single channel reports one scalar wrench component, and no algorithm on that signal can tell a changed physical interaction from a degraded calibration baseline. Without an independent reference, such as an unloaded tare or zero-point proof test, that signal alone cannot establish the drift at runtime.[^fn-hw-piezoresistive-drift]

[^fn-hw-piezoresistive-drift]: **Strain-Gauge Transducer Drift**\index{Strain-gauge transducer!drift}: Mechanical stress relaxation, adhesive creep, and temperature cycles can alter a strain-gauge bridge baseline over extended campaigns. Filtering that signal alone cannot distinguish baseline drift from a true change in force. An unloaded tare, a zero-point proof test, or independently calibrated sensing can supply the reference needed to check the force estimate.

The weakened latch at the door is the arm's case of the same limit, and a faster one. Until the latch yields, the joint torque sensors read the same torques against a weakened latch as against a sound one, because both carry the same contact force, and the channel holds no trace of the strength that remains. The yield is irreversible, and no command issued after it restores the latch, so a faster classifier on the joint torque channel protects nothing. The defensible responses supply what that channel lacks. A proof test establishes the latch's strength at a declared interval, and it covers the interval only if corrosion and wear cannot carry the yield force below the contact ceiling between two tests, a rate that the maintenance record, not the torque channel, must support.

```{python}
#| label: calc-frontier-latch-compliance
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ A SERIES COMPLIANT ELEMENT AT THE DOOR LATCH
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-frontier-passive-compliance-containment,
# │          @eq-frontier-passive-compliance.
# │ Goal:    Size the stiffness and stroke of a series spring that lets the
# │          arm meet the latch at the faster approach speed without passing
# │          the declared force floor, using the registry's latch values.
# │ Show:    rigid-plate result at both approach speeds; the stiffness bound;
# │          the element stiffness, stroke, and the peak if torque is removed.
# │ How:     after the tripwire, the arm travels v t_resp + v^2/(2 a_arm)
# │          (calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile, the Ch10 model); the force
# │          condition F_trip + k_eq * stroke <= F_floor bounds the series
# │          stiffness k_eq; springs in series give the element stiffness; a
# │          coasting mass stores m v^2/2 on top of the tripwire energy.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.physics import calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class LatchCompliance:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Registry and chosen design inputs) ──────────────────────────
    k_plate = AISLE.k_latch  # category: illustrative (strike-plate contact stiffness)
    v_guarded = AISLE.v_latch_approach  # category: illustrative (guarded approach, the declared ODD)
    v_fast = AISLE.v_latch_high  # category: illustrative (faster approach the policy proposes)
    f_trip = AISLE.f_latch_tripwire  # category: chosen (contact tripwire)
    t_resp = AISLE.t_contact_response  # category: illustrative (tripwire to brake onset)
    f_floor = AISLE.f_latch_limit  # category: illustrative (declared force floor, a judgment, not a measured strength)
    m_eff = RM.arm_effective_contact_mass  # category: derived (robot-side effective mass at the TCP)
    f_pre = 0.0 * ureg.newton  # category: chosen (series spring without preload)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    rigid_guarded = calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile(scenario=AISLE)
    rigid_fast = calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile(approach_velocity=v_fast, scenario=AISLE)
    a_arm = rigid_guarded["a_arm_needed"].to(ureg.meter / ureg.second**2)  # hold the arm to the guarded approach's stop
    a_arm_fast_rigid = rigid_fast["a_arm_needed"].to(ureg.meter / ureg.second**2)

    stroke_fast = (v_fast * t_resp + v_fast**2 / (2 * a_arm)).to(ureg.millimeter)  # driven stroke after the tripwire
    k_eq_max = ((f_floor - f_trip) / stroke_fast).to(ureg.newton / ureg.meter)
    k_spring_max = (1 / (1 / k_eq_max - 1 / k_plate)).to(ureg.newton / ureg.meter)
    stroke_needed = ((f_floor - f_pre) / k_spring_max).to(ureg.millimeter)  # element deflection at the floor force

    def coast_peak(k, v, m, f0):
        # Peak force if drive torque is removed at the tripwire: f0^2/(2k) + m v^2/2 = F^2/(2k)
        return (f0**2 + k * m * v**2) ** 0.5

    f_coast_rigid_guarded = coast_peak(k_plate, v_guarded, m_eff, f_trip).to(ureg.newton)
    f_coast_rigid_fast = coast_peak(k_plate, v_fast, m_eff, f_trip).to(ureg.newton)
    f_coast_compliant_fast = coast_peak(k_eq_max, v_fast, m_eff, f_trip).to(ureg.newton)
    check_profile = calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile(approach_velocity=v_fast, latch_stiffness=k_eq_max, scenario=AISLE)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(a_arm.magnitude - 2.9508) < 5e-4, f"Guarded-approach arm stop should be 2.95 m/s^2, got {a_arm}.")
    check(abs(a_arm_fast_rigid.magnitude - 400.0) < 1e-6, f"Rigid plate at the fast approach needs 400 m/s^2, got {a_arm_fast_rigid}.")
    check(abs(stroke_fast.magnitude - 1.8944) < 5e-4, f"Driven stroke at the fast approach should be 1.89 mm, got {stroke_fast}.")
    check(abs(k_eq_max.magnitude - 44868.0) < 5.0, f"Series stiffness bound should be 44.9 kN/m, got {k_eq_max}.")
    check(abs(k_spring_max.magnitude - 50537.0) < 5.0, f"Element stiffness should be 50.5 kN/m, got {k_spring_max}.")
    check(abs(stroke_needed.magnitude - 1.979) < 5e-3, f"Element stroke should be 1.98 mm, got {stroke_needed}.")
    check(k_eq_max < k_plate, "The fast approach needs a softer load path than the rigid plate.")
    check(abs(check_profile["a_arm_needed"].magnitude - a_arm.magnitude) < 1e-6, "With k_eq at the bound, the Ch10 model needs the same arm stop.")
    check(f_coast_rigid_guarded < f_floor, "At the guarded approach the rigid plate stays under the floor even if torque is removed.")
    check(f_coast_rigid_fast > 2 * f_floor, "At the fast approach the rigid plate more than doubles the floor.")
    check(f_coast_compliant_fast < f_floor, "With the element, removing torque at the tripwire stays under the floor.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    k_plate_str = fmt_sci_qty(k_plate, ureg.newton / ureg.meter, precision=1)
    v_guarded_str = fmt_velocity(v_guarded, precision=2)
    v_fast_str = fmt_velocity(v_fast, precision=2)
    f_trip_str = fmt_force(f_trip, precision=0)
    t_resp_str = fmt_latency(t_resp, unit=ureg.ms, precision=0)
    f_floor_str = fmt_force(f_floor, precision=0)
    m_eff_str = fmt_mass(m_eff, unit=ureg.kg, precision=0)
    a_arm_str = fmt_acceleration(a_arm, precision=2)
    a_arm_fast_rigid_str = fmt_acceleration(a_arm_fast_rigid, precision=0)
    stroke_fast_str = fmt_length(stroke_fast, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    k_eq_max_str = fmt_qty(k_eq_max.to(ureg.kilonewton / ureg.meter), unit=ureg.kilonewton / ureg.meter, precision=1)
    k_spring_max_str = fmt_qty(k_spring_max.to(ureg.kilonewton / ureg.meter), unit=ureg.kilonewton / ureg.meter, precision=1)
    stroke_needed_str = fmt_length(stroke_needed, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    f_coast_rigid_guarded_str = fmt_force(f_coast_rigid_guarded, precision=1)
    f_coast_rigid_fast_str = fmt_force(f_coast_rigid_fast, precision=1)
    f_coast_compliant_fast_str = fmt_force(f_coast_compliant_fast, precision=1)
```

A passive compliant element can limit transmitted force over a qualified stroke, the principle behind the series elastic actuator [@pratt1995series] and the mechanical torque limiter. Two conditions govern it, and both concern the stroke the arm *drives* after contact is detected rather than the stroke the element happens to have. After a force tripwire $F_{\text{trip}}$ fires, the arm keeps moving for its response time $t_{\text{resp}}$ and then stops at deceleration $a_{\text{arm}}$, so it drives the load path through $\Delta x_{\text{driven}} = v\,t_{\text{resp}} + v^2/(2a_{\text{arm}})$. The force condition bounds the stiffness $k_{\text{eq}}$ of the whole load path, element and strike plate in series, as @eq-frontier-passive-compliance states:
$$F_{\text{trip}} + k_{\text{eq}}\,\Delta x_{\text{driven}} \le F_{\text{floor}} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad k_{\text{eq}} \le \frac{F_{\text{floor}}-F_{\text{trip}}}{v\,t_{\text{resp}} + v^2/(2a_{\text{arm}})}.$$ {#eq-frontier-passive-compliance}
The stroke condition requires the element's available travel to exceed its deflection at the floor force, $(F_{\text{floor}}-F_{\text{preload}})/k_{\text{spring}}$, so that it never bottoms out and hands the load to the rigid path. $F_{\text{floor}}$ is not the latch's strength, which this section has just shown is unmeasured between proof tests. It is the declared floor on that strength, an accountable judgment recorded with its status.

The door latch shows what the bound buys. At the guarded `{python} LatchCompliance.v_guarded_str` approach, the `{python} LatchCompliance.k_plate_str` strike plate already satisfies @eq-frontier-passive-compliance with an arm stop of `{python} LatchCompliance.a_arm_str`, the premise @sec-intent-handoff derived. At the faster `{python} LatchCompliance.v_fast_str` approach the same rigid plate would need `{python} LatchCompliance.a_arm_fast_rigid_str`, which no arm supplies, so that approach is refused. Holding the arm to the guarded stop instead, the arm drives `{python} LatchCompliance.stroke_fast_str` after the `{python} LatchCompliance.f_trip_str` tripwire, which bounds the load path at `{python} LatchCompliance.k_eq_max_str`. Springs in series add compliances, $1/k_{\text{eq}} = 1/k_{\text{spring}} + 1/k_{\text{plate}}$, because both carry the same force and their deflections add. In series with the plate, that calls for an element no stiffer than `{python} LatchCompliance.k_spring_max_str` with at least `{python} LatchCompliance.stroke_needed_str` of travel against the `{python} LatchCompliance.f_floor_str` floor.

The quasi-static bound assumes the drive keeps braking. If the response is to remove drive torque instead, the `{python} LatchCompliance.m_eff_str` effective mass coasts into the spring, and energy balance gives the peak. A spring compressed to force $F$ stores $F^2/(2k_{\text{eq}})$; at the tripwire it already holds $F_{\text{trip}}^2/(2k_{\text{eq}})$, and the coasting mass adds its kinetic energy $m_{\text{eff}}v^2/2$, so the peak is $\sqrt{F_{\text{trip}}^2 + k_{\text{eq}}\,m_{\text{eff}}\,v^2}$, the dynamic term that dominates fast impacts [@haddadin2009requirements]. With the element that peak is `{python} LatchCompliance.f_coast_compliant_fast_str`; against the bare plate it would be `{python} LatchCompliance.f_coast_rigid_fast_str` at the fast approach and `{python} LatchCompliance.f_coast_rigid_guarded_str` at the guarded one. The element therefore bounds the force delivered to whatever strength the latch has, which is the right response to a premise the torque channel cannot observe. It does not establish that strength, and qualification must still test the complete load path, damping, and response, not stiffness alone.[^fn-math-contact-lipschitz]

The latch, the floor film, and the packaging tab end in the same place. Where a premise cannot be observed before the deadline, the engineer chooses among a probe, a conservative action, a passive limit, a proof test, and a narrower claim by the claim each supports and the evidence needed to maintain it. Each choice also names the evidence that would lift it, and that evidence is what the next capability must buy.

[^fn-math-contact-lipschitz]: **Contact Boundary**\index{Contact mechanics!non-smooth impact}: Rigid impact and friction transitions can invalidate a smooth free-motion model. Peak contact force and component damage require measured stiffness, damping, geometry, and actuator response; neither a controller nor a passive part alone supplies a universal bound.

## Choosing the Next Capability {#sec-frontier-assumptions-change}

The packaging cell's restricted transport and refused sign-off lead to different research investments. Faster proposal serving may improve throughput; a qualified engagement measurement may support autonomous sign-off. Each advance needs a predeclared task result and a test of the premise it changes. Improvement within an existing envelope and evidence for expanding that envelope are related but distinct outcomes.

### What a restriction costs {#sec-frontier-deployment-economics}

```{python}
#| label: calc-frontier-restriction-cost
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE PRICE OF A RESTRICTION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-frontier-deployment-economics.
# │ Goal:    Price the oil-film entry's restricted mode in the one unit that
# │          holds on every site, time per aisle leg, and set it beside the
# │          size of the campaigns that would retire it.
# │ Show:    the speed cut, cruise time per leg at both speeds, the added time,
# │          and the closure and coverage campaign sizes from the cells above.
# │ How:     cruise time = leg length / speed (acceleration and stops omitted,
# │          so the figure is a lower bound on the added time).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class RestrictionCost:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_nominal = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen (normal-mode aisle speed)
    v_restricted = OilFilm.v_restricted  # category: chosen (restricted mode on inspected floors)
    leg = AISLE.aisle_length  # category: illustrative (aisle length)
    totes_reported = 100_000  # category: measured, vendor-reported (Agility Robotics, 20 Nov 2025: Digit at GXO Flowery Branch)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    speed_cut = (1 - v_restricted / v_nominal).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    t_leg_nominal = (leg / v_nominal).to(ureg.second)
    t_leg_restricted = (leg / v_restricted).to(ureg.second)
    t_leg_added = (t_leg_restricted - t_leg_nominal).to(ureg.second)
    time_increase = (t_leg_added / t_leg_nominal).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(speed_cut - 0.2308) < 5e-4, f"Speed cut should be 23.1 percent, got {speed_cut}.")
    check(abs(t_leg_nominal.magnitude - 23.077) < 5e-3, f"Nominal leg should take 23.1 s, got {t_leg_nominal}.")
    check(abs(t_leg_restricted.magnitude - 30.0) < 1e-9, f"Restricted leg should take 30.0 s, got {t_leg_restricted}.")
    check(abs(time_increase - 0.30) < 1e-9, f"Leg time should rise 30 percent, got {time_increase}.")
    check(time_increase > speed_cut, "A speed cut lengthens the leg by more than its own percentage.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_nominal_str = fmt_velocity(v_nominal, precision=1)
    v_restricted_str = fmt_velocity(v_restricted, precision=0)
    leg_str = fmt_length(leg, unit=ureg.meter, precision=0)
    speed_cut_str = fmt_percent(speed_cut, precision=1, style="prose")
    t_leg_nominal_str = fmt_latency(t_leg_nominal, unit=ureg.second, precision=1)
    t_leg_restricted_str = fmt_latency(t_leg_restricted, unit=ureg.second, precision=0)
    time_increase_str = fmt_percent(time_increase, precision=0, style="prose")
    totes_reported_str = fmt_int(totes_reported, commas=True)
```

Every entry in the register buys protection with throughput, and that price has so far gone unstated. The oil-film entry's restricted mode lowers the aisle speed from `{python} RestrictionCost.v_nominal_str` to `{python} RestrictionCost.v_restricted_str`, a speed cut of `{python} RestrictionCost.speed_cut_str`. At cruise it lengthens each `{python} RestrictionCost.leg_str` aisle leg from `{python} RestrictionCost.t_leg_nominal_str` to `{python} RestrictionCost.t_leg_restricted_str`, `{python} RestrictionCost.time_increase_str` more time per leg before acceleration and stops are counted. Time rises by more than speed falls because travel time scales as $1/v$.

The restriction stands until its closure test passes, and that test has a price of its own, the `{python} OilFilm.n_closure_str` seeded-film trials of the register entry, or the `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.n_coverage_str` seeded hazardous proposals that a shield's coverage claim requires. The register therefore leaves the engineer an economic decision as well as a technical one. A closure test is worth running when the throughput the restriction costs over the period it would otherwise persist exceeds the cost of the campaign and of the instrument it qualifies. A restriction is the better choice when its premise is cheap to maintain operationally, as a spill procedure on a few pallet-jack routes may be. Both sides of that comparison are site data: the value of a completed task, the machine's duty hours on the restricted routes, and the cost per trial of the campaign. This example supplies none of them, so it prices the restriction in time, the unit that transfers to every site.

The same accounting governs deployment as a whole. A humanoid deployment in logistics that its operator called the industry's first was contracted as robots-as-a-service in 2024 [@gxo2024agility], and such deployments are reported by volume moved, `{python} RestrictionCost.totes_reported_str` totes at one site by November 2025 by the vendor's count [@agility2025totes]. In that setting every intervention, restriction, and withheld mode appears as lost throughput, and the release decisions of @sec-release become operating costs. Intervention rate is priced twice. Each human takeover consumes operator time, and a fleet that needs frequent takeovers can serve only routes where an operator is available. A defensible business case therefore reports proposer autonomy, whole-machine task success, and protective responses separately, as the first fallacy below insists, because each carries a different price.

### Who bears the costs that safety does not count {#sec-frontier-workforce-accountability}

The accounting above prices a restriction in machine time. Deployment also moves costs onto people, and no product-safety claim measures them. On the warehouse machine the work around a tote move does not disappear. It moves to the operators who take over when the proposer stalls (@sec-intervention), who clear and inspect the restricted routes, and who maintain the register's standing conditions. The intervention rate that release measures is therefore also the description of a job: how often a person must be available, where, and with how much warning. The aggregate effect has been estimated only for an earlier generation of machines. Across US local labor markets, greater exposure to fixed industrial robots after 1990 reduced both employment and wages [@acemoglu2020robots]. Whether mobile manipulators in logistics repeat that pattern has not been measured. The records this book builds supply the site-level counts such a study would need, such as tasks moved, takeovers, and operator hours on each route.

Accountability extends past product safety for the same reason. Conformity under the Machinery Regulation answers whether the machine may be operated near the people around it; it does not answer who answers for how its records are used. The warehouse machine's authority log and black-box recorder name the operator behind every takeover. A system that used those records to score operators would itself be a high-risk AI system under the EU AI Act, whose Annex III lists systems intended to monitor and evaluate the performance and behavior of persons in work relationships, and whose Article 26 requires an employer to inform workers' representatives and the affected workers before putting such a system into use at the workplace [@eu2024aiact]. The architectural answer is the one this book gives for every premise. Each record declares its purpose, its owner, and who may read it, and release treats those declarations as standing conditions (@sec-release-recorded-people), so that a record created to reconstruct an incident is not silently repurposed to evaluate a worker. The machine's effects on its workforce then have a named owner, like every other residual claim.

### Proposal is not permission, in law {#sec-frontier-thesis-in-law}

The book's third law, that a learned proposal is not permission, becomes a legal requirement for machinery sold in the European Union. The Machinery Regulation, whose dates and scope the standards map of @sec-release-standards-map sets out, lists safety components "with fully or partially self-evolving behaviour using machine learning approaches ensuring safety functions," and machinery that embeds them, among the categories whose conformity a notified body must assess (Annex I, Part A) [@eu2023machinery]. Its essential requirements add the operational half: the limits of safety functions are established in the manufacturer's risk assessment, and no setting or rule the machine generates, including during a learning phase, may change where the change could lead to a hazardous situation (Annex III, section 1.2.1).

Read against this book's architecture, the regulation draws the proposal boundary in law. The question it turns on is whether a learned component ensures a safety function. A learned proposer whose output reaches the actuators only through an independent permission path with fixed, signed limits does not. The safety functions are then carried by safety-rated parts that contain no learned component: the drive functions and safety scanner of @tbl-12-certified-functions, and the safety MCU's lease-expiry watchdog, which commands STO or SS1 on the drives when permission lapses. The admission checks that shape each proposal, such as the barrier projection and the feasibility and freshness tests, are not claimed as a safety function, and their limits are set by the risk assessment rather than learned. A learned component that does ensure one, such as a learned person detector used as the protective function or a policy whose commands reach the drives without independent admission, falls under Annex I, Part A and needs third-party assessment. The architecture therefore helps decide the conformity route, though for a particular machine that reading rests with the manufacturer's risk assessment and, for Part A categories, the notified body. The residual-claims register records what section 1.2.1 asks for, the declared limits with the evidence behind them and the conditions under which an update may not change them. How a notified body will assess a learned component whose behavior depends on its training data remains open as of 2026, and the last problem below returns to it.

### Match the experiment to the missing evidence {#sec-frontier-four-gap-classes}

An unmeasured observable calls for a measurement that distinguishes the relevant states before action becomes ineffective. An evaluation deficit calls for trials or estimators that represent the claimed population, with uncertainty and dependence accounted for. A theoretical deficit calls for a bounded argument whose assumptions can be established for the machine. A scope mismatch calls for a changed architecture or a narrower task. These diagnoses choose the next experiment; they do not force every residual claim to have a detector-based solution.

Applied to the register, the classes separate the open premises cleanly. The oil film, the walking person, the object's identity, and the packaging tab are unmeasured observables, and each calls for a qualified sensing channel or a restriction that removes the need for one. The loaded dispatch-to-admission timing and the shield's coverage $c_h$ are evaluation deficits, closed by trials sampled from the states that matter. The premises of a formal certificate about the plant are a theoretical deficit (@sec-verification-formal-limits), and autonomous package sign-off with the available camera is a scope mismatch, repaired by downstream inspection or a narrower claim.

The tail methods collected in @sec-appendix-ml-evt can help evaluate rare exceedances when their distributional assumptions hold. A fitted tail does not establish those assumptions or validate unobserved contact dynamics. Likewise, the reachability methods in @sec-appendix-control-hj-reachability concern a specified plant and disturbance model. Moving an unsupported friction premise into a simulator or certificate does not discharge it.

### Research that changes an engineering result {#sec-frontier-four-open-challenges}

The open problems that matter to a physical AI engineer are the ones whose solution would change a verdict in a release argument. Six stand out as of 2026. Each stresses one of the four laws, sits in one of the gap classes above, and has a recognizable form of progress. @Tbl-17-frontier-agenda sets them side by side with dated instances of current work; the paragraphs below state the durable question behind each.

Generalist and cross-embodiment policies change what "the proposer's limits" means. A single pretrained vision-language-action model now serves many bodies. One flow-matching policy was trained across single-arm, dual-arm, and mobile platforms [@black2024pi0], building on pooled cross-embodiment data (@sec-data-cross-embodiment), and newer systems improve from their own deployments through reinforcement learning with human corrections [@physicalintelligence2025recap] or transfer motion between embodiments [@geminirobotics2025gemini15]. Evidence gathered on one body does not obviously transfer to another, and a proposer that keeps learning in the field is a moving target for release evidence collected on an earlier version (@sec-release-deployment-lifecycle). The open question is how evidence for a shared model transfers across bodies and across updates. Progress would be a transfer argument with a stated equivalence condition, tested by predicting a new body's closed-loop failure rate before measuring it. The trend raises the value of the permission path, whose limits are set per body and do not change when the shared proposer does.

Data scaling is the quantitative frontier of the second law. The largest controlled study so far, over forty thousand demonstrations on real robots, found that generalization to new environments and objects followed a roughly power-law relationship in the number of distinct environments and objects, while further demonstrations per environment beyond a threshold added little [@lin2025datascaling]. Diversity, not volume, answers which demonstrations to collect (@sec-data-scaling-frontier). The open question is whether such laws hold for contact-rich, long-horizon, and safety-relevant behavior, where rare states matter most and the machine's own actions choose what it sees next. Progress would be scaling curves measured on closed-loop failure rates inside a declared ODD, not only on average success.

World models as evaluators attack the exposure wall. Learned video and latent world models are now trained as general-purpose predictors of the physical world [@nvidia2025cosmos; @assran2025vjepa2], and some are built specifically to evaluate robot policies, with reported close agreement with real-robot evaluation on the tasks studied [@jeon2026roboworld]. Model rollouts are cheap where physical trials are not. The durable limit is the third fallacy below. A model cannot supply an observable absent from its inputs or a contact property absent from its training data. The open question is when a learned simulator's evaluation counts as evidence, and for which claims. Progress would be a stated proxy-transfer condition, in the sense of @sec-evaluation-proxy-transfer-law, validated on the failure tail rather than on average success, with the model's own provenance recorded as for any simulator component (@sec-training-simulator-component).

Dynamically stable machines are where the first law bites hardest, and they close the humanoid thread this book has followed at the end of each part. Perspectives \ref{capstone-nervous-humanoid-crucible}, \ref{capstone-evaluation-humanoid-crucible}, \ref{capstone-placement-humanoid-crucible}, and \ref{capstone-release-humanoid-crucible} found that every stage of the argument carries over to a balancing robot except the fallback. A recovery step replaces the stop, and refusal needs a powered descent or a supported hold rather than de-energization. Functional safety practice assumes the opposite. Its certifiable reaction is the removal of power, and for a walking biped that reaction is itself the hazard, a mismatch recent work calls the fail-passive gap [@ding2026failpassive]. The open problem is a safe state that is actively controlled yet certifiable. Progress would be a reaction chain, certified like a braking function, that reaches a supported rest state from any admitted gait phase within a measured energy budget. The most capable learned machines are also the ones for which "stop" is hardest to define.

Contact-rich and dexterous manipulation turns on the chapter's canonical hidden variable, contact state, whether the latch yields, the tab engages, or the jar crushes. Joint torque and vision report it poorly. Tactile sensing is the observable most likely to close it, and vision-based tactile sensors already resolve contact geometry and force at the fingertip [@yuan2017gelsight]. The third law then asks what the permission path can verify about contact, where force rises within milliseconds of touch (@sec-enforcement-intentional-contact) and compliance may be the only response fast enough (@sec-frontier-passive-compliance-containment). Progress would be a tactile channel qualified like any detector, with a stated miss rate for slip or incipient yield, feeding a contact controller whose force bound the permission path can check [@tedrake2023manipulation].

Certifying learned safety functions is the fourth law's open problem. The regulation of @sec-frontier-thesis-in-law asks notified bodies to assess machine-learning components that ensure safety functions, yet no accepted method establishes such a component's failure rate at the confidence a safety function needs. Formal verification of a neural network proves properties of the declared network [@katz2017reluplex] but inherits the premises of @sec-verification-formal-limits. Statistical evidence meets the exposure wall. A safety filter moves the claim onto the filter's own coverage, as the shield calculation showed [@hsu2024safetyfilter]. The open problem is a combined argument, formal where the model is exact and statistical where it is not, with its confidence budgeted across the parts. Until one exists, keeping the learned component outside the safety function remains the defensible default. Progress would be a published conformity assessment of a learned safety component together with its argument.

\Needspace{24\baselineskip}

| Open problem                              | Law stressed               | Gap class             | Progress would be                                                                      | State of practice, as of 2026                                                                                                                                                                        |
|:------------------------------------------|:---------------------------|:----------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Generalist, cross-embodiment policies** | Evidence bounds authority  | Evaluation deficit    | Evidence that transfers across bodies and updates under a stated equivalence condition | One policy across several robot types [@black2024pi0]; learning from deployment with corrections [@physicalintelligence2025recap]; motion transfer between embodiments [@geminirobotics2025gemini15] |
| **Data scaling**                          | Endogenous data            | Evaluation deficit    | Scaling curves on closed-loop failure rates inside a declared ODD                      | Roughly power-law gains in environment and object diversity, saturating in demonstrations per environment [@lin2025datascaling]                                                                      |
| **World models as evaluators**            | Evidence bounds authority  | Evaluation deficit    | A proxy-transfer condition validated on the failure tail                               | General world foundation models [@nvidia2025cosmos; @assran2025vjepa2]; a world model built for policy evaluation [@jeon2026roboworld]                                                               |
| **Fall-safe dynamically stable machines** | Irreversibility            | Scope mismatch        | A certified, actively controlled reaction chain to a supported rest state              | The fail-passive gap located in a humanoid pick-and-place cell [@ding2026failpassive]                                                                                                                |

: **A research agenda keyed to the four laws, as of 2026**: Each row names an open problem, the law it stresses, the gap class of @sec-frontier-four-gap-classes it belongs to, and the evidence that would count as progress. The last column dates the state of practice and should be refreshed in later editions; the durable content is in the first four columns. {#tbl-17-frontier-agenda tbl-colwidths="[18,15,14,25,28]"}

Two older problems run through all six. An adapting proposer, whether it retrains on fleet data or adapts online to wear and terrain [@kumar2021rma], is the moving target of the first problem, and its update must not consume resources the permission path needs. Multi-robot coordination couples permission paths. Delayed shared intent cannot replace the local observations each admission needs, and a shared payload couples the robots' forces. Each direction extends the same engineering discipline rather than suspending it. The next capability begins with a concrete task the current machine cannot yet perform, an identified constraint or missing premise, and evidence that would justify the changed design.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-frontier-fallacies-pitfalls}

The warehouse and packaging examples can fail as engineering arguments even when their individual calculations are correct. Three mistakes sever the connection between useful work, physical limits, and evidence.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *A protective intervention means the whole machine failed its task.*

A least-change speed correction may let the robot complete its delivery within the permitted envelope. Report raw proposer autonomy separately from whole-machine task success and protective outcomes. Combining them into one failure count obscures whether the next improvement belongs in learning, integration, or the protective response.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Treating a restriction as evidence that its physical premise holds.*

The oil-film calculation still needs traction after the speed ceiling is reduced. Inspection must have a qualified means of establishing the restricted friction floor and a regime that preserves it; a visually clear route or a signed speed value supplies neither by itself. The actual illustrative release remains refused, while the stipulated service branch demonstrates the consequence of supporting those premises.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *More model capacity or simulated exposure settles every residual claim.*

A better proposer can improve useful behavior, and simulation can expose failures in modeled conditions. Neither supplies a physical observable absent from its inputs or validates a contact property omitted by its model. Select new experience, measurement, a passive limit, or a narrower task according to the missing claim, then evaluate the changed machine.
:::

## Summary {#sec-frontier-summary}

The warehouse mission now has a connected design argument, and the packaging cell shows how to transfer it. Physical budgets define feasible action; traceable experience and closed-loop evaluation establish useful behavior; timely integration preserves that behavior within current limits; release and maintenance keep the service tied to its evidence. The residual-claims register preserves what remains open and directs the next improvement. It also gives an owner to costs that no safety claim measures, the operator work a deployment creates and the use of records that identify workers.

The book opened by asking why a better prediction can still produce a worse physical action. This chapter's evidence answers it. A better proposer cannot supply the friction premise that the oil film removes, because no input it receives reports that friction. It cannot make a derated mode evaluated, because the restriction that shortens the stop also moves the proposer into states its evaluation never sampled. It cannot close a detectorless claim such as the glare-hidden tab, because the observation that would support the claim does not exist. In each case the action is judged by physics, timing, and evidence that the prediction does not contain, which is why the book has treated the learned model as one component of a machine rather than as the machine. The rest of the machine supplies what the prediction lacks, one law at a time: physical budgets under irreversibility, closed-loop evidence of competence under endogenous data, an independent permission path under proposal is not permission, and a release bounded by evidence under the fourth law. As learned models take the last steps toward the actuator, the permission decision stays outside them, and the residual-claims register names the evidence each next capability must supply.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Engineering a machine that senses and acts"}

* **Useful service joins the four laws:** Body limits, learned competence, independent permission, and maintained evidence must support the same task; a better prediction strengthens only one link of that argument.
* **Competence can grow:** New qualified experience, retraining, and regression evaluation can extend what the next candidate can justify.
* **Admission can preserve success:** A minimally corrected proposal can complete useful work; proposer autonomy, task success, and protection require separate measures.
* **Restrictions need evidence:** A lower speed still needs traction, clearance, and a feasible response. A stipulated supported branch teaches the release decision without turning illustrative records into measurements.
* **Residual limits select the next experiment:** Missing observations, evaluation support, proof premises, and task scope call for different engineering responses.
:::

A physical AI engineer can carry an intended task through this entire chain. The engineer derives an action envelope from the body and its environment, develops a learned proposer from traceable data, and evaluates that proposer in the closed loop it will inhabit. The engineer then integrates sensing, state, intent, and planning with an independent permission path, measures its timing and fallback behavior, and tests the complete machine under declared operating conditions. The release decision joins useful capability to the evidence that supports it. When evidence is missing, the engineer can identify whether the next step is a measurement, a learning experiment, an architectural change, or a narrower task. @Sec-boundary promised the ability to design, teach, integrate, evaluate, and maintain such a machine within justified operating limits, and to name, when the evidence is incomplete, what would support the next capability. That ability to build and justify a machine that senses and acts is the discipline this book develops.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From physical AI to the systems discipline"}
The next unfamiliar machine will bring a different body, task, and environment. Its engineering begins by tracing how observations become proposals and how admitted commands become force, motion, and heat. The methods developed here provide a way to teach useful behavior, integrate it with timely physical control, and determine which operating claims the resulting evidence supports. This work is dedicated to the students, researchers, and systems engineers who take up the challenge of giving machines safe and capable hands in an open physical world.
:::
